2.text: to note that of late years, in the families of rich Maritime merchants of the

3.text: east shore, some faint realization of these ideas has come to life, partly per-

4.text: haps through the influence of these tales. For instance, three daughters of

5.text: Kuvaˊr, the Eskimo merchant of Indian Point,¹ had something of the character

6.text: of the secluded beauty. They were kept, not in the iron box, but in the

7.text: large sleeping-room of their father’s house. When talked to by strange men,

8.text: they pretended to be shy, and not inclined to conversation. Even the color

9.text: of their face grew more delicate and white, as becomes a secluded beauty.

10.text: All their time and attention were given to needle-work on soft, spotted skins.

11.text: Of those skins they prepared man’s clothes of the best quality. Of course

12.text: these clothes were sold to American whalers in exchange for sugar, flour, and

13.text: cheap brandy, which does not correspond to the description given in tales.

14.text: The other type of Chukchee bride, as described in tales, corresponds

15.text: more closely to the conditions of Chukchee life. She is strong and proud.

16.text: Not either of her parents, but she herself, shows resistance to the suitor.

17.text: She has to be sought for and conquered by strength and courage.

18.text: In one tale the bride is described as living in a single house with her

19.text: old parents. She refuses all suitors. Being very swift of foot, she invites

20.text: them to a foot-race, in which they are defeated. Then they are sent home.

21.text: At last a young man comes to her house. He drives his spear into the

22.text: ground in front of the door, and enters. The girl is not there. Her father

23.text: inquires, “Why have you come?” — “I am a suitor.” — “We have a daughter;

24.text: but she is proud, very light of foot, and she invites her suitors to a foot-race.”

25.text: Then the old man looks into the face of the young man, and asks him, “Is

26.text: she going to outdo you too?” — “I do not know. Maybe she will.” The

27.text: girl comes home from the herd. “Oh, oh! whose spear is standing here

28.text: before our door?” The mother says, “Do not speak so loud!” — “No, no, let

29.text: him beat me in a foot-race!” She enters the tent. Her braids are very long

30.text: and heavy. They reach to her ankles and almost sweep the ground. Imme-

31.text: diately after her coming, she changes her clothes and puts on breeches and

32.text: a racing-dress. The father says, “He is weary and cannot run just now.” —

33.text: “No, no! let us race now.” They go out and start. The girl is far ahead.

34.text: She passes the last hill on their course. She is already on the home stretch.

35.text: Both are on the home stretch, but she is still in the lead. When they are

36.text: running down a slope, she teases him, saying, “Can you not outrun me at

37.text: least here” — “No, I am too tired!” But his toes are already upon her

38.text: heels. He too is light of foot.

39.text: When they are descending another slope, he overtakes her and passes

40.text: her. Then he speeds forward swifter than an arrow. The long red tassel

41.text: hanging on his back stretches back straight as a reed. The two braids of

42.text: the girl also stretch back as straight as two arrows. He looks back over his
